content: The Regional Health Authorities (RHFs) in Norway are state enterprises tasked with managing specialist healthcare services within one of the four designated regions of the country. Their responsibilities encompass patient treatment, the education and training of medical personnel, conducting research, and providing training for both patients and their relatives. The scope of their operations includes hospitals, psychiatric care, ambulance services, hospital pharmacies, emergency telephone services, and laboratories. The actual delivery of healthcare services is carried out by subsidiary health trusts (HFs), which typically consist of one or more hospitals and their associated responsibilities. These Regional Health Authorities operate under the jurisdiction of the Norwegian Ministry of Health and Care Services. The Regional Health Authorities were established on January 1, 2002, as part of a healthcare reform in which the Norwegian government assumed responsibility for hospitals from the counties. Initially, five authorities were created, but in 2007, the Southern and Eastern Norway authorities were merged. This reform was spearheaded by the then-Minister of Health, Tore Tønne, who served for only a year and a half. The primary objective of the reform was to enhance the efficiency of hospital operations and reduce the costs associated with specialist healthcare services, which, by 2007, had an annual budget of NOK 114 billion, accounting for approximately 14% of the state budget. The reform has faced criticism on several fronts. Tore Tønne, who had a corporate management background from Statoil and the Aker Group, introduced elements of corporate governance and public tendering into Norway's healthcare system. Critics have labeled this approach as market fundamentalism, arguing that it prioritized economic considerations over other factors. This was exacerbated by the initial decision to exclude politicians from the boards of the authorities and trusts, effectively removing political oversight from healthcare services. Consequently, decisions such as hospital closures could be made without political resolution. The Second Stoltenberg Cabinet later amended this policy by appointing politicians to the boards of the authorities. Further criticism has been directed at the organizational structure of the authorities. The reform introduced additional layers of administration—government, regional health authority, health trust, and hospital—where previously there had been only two levels: county and hospital. Additionally, the administrative offices of the authorities were often located in towns outside major regional centers, some of which lacked hospitals, complicating the recruitment of management personnel. This has led to escalating director salaries, comparable to those in the corporate sector. Moreover, due to reductions in government funding, the authorities have accumulated significant debt. The Central Norway Regional Health Authority oversees several subsidiaries, including the Central Norway Pharmaceutical Trust, Nordmøre and Romsdal Hospital Trust, Nord-Trøndelag Hospital Trust, St. Olav's Hospital Trust, and Sunnmøre Hospital Trust. These entities are responsible for delivering healthcare services within their respective regions.
